description: Metal extraction by displacement and biological methods, life cycle assessments, and recycling.
content_html:
Atom Economy and Percentage Yield

In industrial chemistry, two key measures tell us how efficiently a reaction uses its raw materials. Atom economy tells you what fraction of the mass of the reactants ends up as the wanted product rather than waste. A high atom economy means less waste is generated, lowering environmental impact and production costs.

The formula is:

$$\text{atom economy} = \frac{M_r \text{ of desired product}}{\text{sum of } M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100$$

Percentage yield compares the actual amount of product made to the theoretical maximum:

$$\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100$$

Percentage yield is often below 100% because of incomplete reactions, side reactions, reversible reactions that do not go to completion, or product lost during purification. The limiting reactant determines the theoretical yield — once it runs out, the reaction stops regardless of how much of the other reactant remains.

Key Fact

Atom economy measures what proportion of reactant atoms become the desired product (from the balanced equation). Percentage yield measures how much product was actually made compared to the theoretical maximum. Both should be as high as possible for economic and environmental reasons.

Life Cycle Assessments

A life cycle assessment (LCA) evaluates the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life. The four main stages are: (1) extracting and processing raw materials, (2) manufacturing, (3) using the product (including transport and packaging), and (4) disposing of the product at the end of its useful life.

LCAs consider: energy consumption at each stage, raw material use, water use, emissions to air and water (including greenhouse gases and toxic substances), waste produced, and the potential for recycling or reuse at the end of life. However, some factors — such as visual impact, noise, or local ecosystem disruption — are difficult to quantify precisely. This means LCAs involve some subjective judgement, and different analysts can reach different conclusions if they weight factors differently. Companies sometimes use selective LCA data to support marketing claims, so evaluating LCA evidence critically is important.

Recycling

Recycling reduces the need to extract new raw materials, saves energy, and reduces the volume of waste going to landfill. Factors that affect decisions about recycling include: the cost of collection and sorting, the energy needed to process recycled material compared to making new material, the market value of the recycled product, and public willingness to separate and recycle materials.

Metals are particularly worth recycling because mining and refining metal ores is very energy-intensive. Recycling aluminium, for example, uses only a small fraction of the energy required to extract aluminium from its ore (bauxite) by electrolysis. Glass and paper can also be recycled effectively, though the economic viability depends on collection costs, sorting complexity and market conditions.

Key Fact

Recycling conserves finite resources, reduces energy use, and cuts landfill waste. Metals such as aluminium are especially valuable to recycle because extracting them from ore by electrolysis is very energy-intensive. The overall benefit must weigh the energy and cost of collection and processing.

Extracting Metals from Low-Grade Ores

Traditional smelting requires high concentrations of metal ore and generates significant environmental impact. Where ore is too dilute (low-grade) to make smelting economically viable, alternative biological methods can be used. Two techniques are particularly important: phytomining and bioleaching.

Phytomining uses plants that can absorb and accumulate metal ions from the soil through their root systems. These plants, sometimes called hyperaccumulators, concentrate metal ions in their leaves and stems. The plants are then harvested and burned; the resulting ash contains a much higher concentration of the metal compound than the original soil. The metal is then extracted from the ash, often by smelting or chemical treatment. The process is slow (growing the plants takes time) but has a lower environmental impact than traditional opencast mining.

Bioleaching uses bacteria that produce acidic solutions (leachate) by reacting with metal sulfide ores. The leachate dissolves the metal compounds out of the ore. The resulting metal-rich solution (often called the ‘pregnant leach solution’) can then have the metal extracted from it either by displacement (adding a more reactive metal) or by electrolysis. Bioleaching is also slower than conventional extraction but requires less energy input and can process waste heaps and low-grade ores that would otherwise be uneconomical to use.

Key Fact

Phytomining uses plants to absorb metal ions; the plants are burned and the metal extracted from the ash. Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce acidic solutions that dissolve metals from low-grade ores; the metal is then removed by displacement or electrolysis. Both are slower but more sustainable alternatives to conventional smelting for low-grade ores.

Traditional reduction with carbon is used for metals below carbon in the reactivity series (such as iron, zinc and copper). Carbon displaces the metal from its oxide when heated at high temperatures. Electrolysis is required for metals above carbon in the reactivity series (such as aluminium) because they cannot be displaced by carbon. Electrolysis uses large amounts of electrical energy, making it expensive. By contrast, phytomining and bioleaching require very little energy but are slow, making them best suited to low-grade or dilute ore bodies where faster methods are not viable.

Sustainability in Chemistry

The principles of sustainable chemistry combine all the ideas above: maximising atom economy to reduce waste, conducting LCAs to guide product design, recycling where possible to conserve finite resources, and using biological or lower-energy extraction methods where appropriate. Chemistry plays a central role in meeting the needs of the present without depleting resources that future generations will need.
exam_tip_html: For 6-mark extended-response questions comparing extraction methods or evaluating LCAs, make sure you give both advantages and disadvantages for each method. ‘Evaluate’ means you must weigh up the evidence and reach a conclusion. For calculation questions involving atom economy or percentage yield, always show the formula, substitution and units. A common error is confusing these two measures — remember: atom economy comes from the balanced equation alone; percentage yield requires actual and theoretical values from the experiment.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Atom economy measures the proportion of reactant mass that becomes the desired product; percentage yield measures how much of the theoretical maximum was actually obtained. Both should be maximised in green chemistry.
  • Life cycle assessments evaluate the environmental impact of a product from raw material extraction through to disposal. They are partly subjective and must be interpreted critically.
  • Phytomining (using plants) and bioleaching (using bacteria) are sustainable alternatives to conventional smelting for low-grade copper ores, requiring less energy but more time.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct formula for percentage yield?
A) (Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all products) × 100
B) (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100
C) (theoretical yield ÷ actual yield) × 100
D) (actual yield ÷ Mr of desired product) × 100
State one advantage and one disadvantage of bioleaching compared to traditional smelting.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of: Advantage — e.g. requires less energy / can extract metal from low-grade ores that are uneconomical to smelt / lower environmental impact from land disturbance. Disadvantage — e.g. the process is very slow / produces acidic leachate that must be managed carefully / yield per unit time is lower than smelting. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how phytomining is used to extract copper from low-grade ore.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Plants (hyperaccumulators) absorb copper ions from the soil through their roots and accumulate them in their tissues; the plants are then harvested and burned; the resulting ash contains a concentrated copper compound which is processed to extract the copper. All three stages described correctly with accurate scientific language.
Secure: Two of the three stages described correctly with mostly accurate language.
Developing: One stage described with some accuracy; limited chemical detail.
Emerging: A general statement about using plants; no process detail. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A reaction to produce calcium oxide has a theoretical yield of 56 g. Only 42 g is actually obtained. Calculate the percentage yield. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Correct formula (1): percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100. Correct substitution (1): (42 ÷ 56) × 100. Correct answer (1): 75%. Correct unit or confirmation that percentage requires no unit (1). [4 marks — common error: dividing theoretical by actual instead of actual by theoretical]

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer produces a polymer by reacting two monomers. The only product is the desired polymer. Explain why the atom economy for this reaction is 100%, and explain why the percentage yield might still be less than 100%.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Atom economy is 100% because all the reactant atoms end up in the single product (no by-products are formed in the balanced equation); percentage yield can still be below 100% because the reaction may be incomplete, product may be lost during processing, or a reversible reaction may not go fully to completion.
Secure: Both concepts distinguished with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: One concept explained correctly; the other confused or missing.
Emerging: States that both measures relate to yield without distinguishing them. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Life cycle assessments always give an objective picture of a product's environmental impact.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Thorough explanation that LCAs cover all four stages (raw materials, manufacture, use, disposal) and consider multiple environmental factors (energy, emissions, water, waste); however they involve subjective weighting of different factors, and data may be incomplete or selectively reported by companies for marketing purposes. A balanced conclusion reached.
Secure: LCAs explained with two or more stages covered; one or two limitations discussed; conclusion present.
Developing: LCAs described at a basic level; limited or no discussion of subjectivity.
Emerging: A general statement about LCAs with little accurate detail. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What does a high atom economy indicate about a chemical reaction?
options: Most reactants were not used up
Most of the reactant mass ends up as the desired product
The actual yield was close to the theoretical yield
The reaction was carried out at high temperature

knowledge_checks.q: Which biological extraction method uses bacteria to dissolve metal compounds from low-grade ores?
In phytomining, plants absorb metal ions through their roots; the plants are then harvested and _____ to produce ash containing concentrated metal compounds.
A life cycle assessment evaluates the environmental impact of a product from raw material extraction to _____.
options: disposal at the end of its life

knowledge_checks.q: Match each term to its correct description:
right: Compares actual product obtained to the theoretical maximum
The reactant that runs out first and determines maximum product
The proportion of reactant atoms that become the desired product

flashcard_questions.a: The proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product, calculated from the balanced equation.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the formula for percentage yield?
Why might percentage yield be below 100%?
flashcard_questions.a: Incomplete reaction, side reactions, product lost during processing, or a reversible reaction not going to completion.
The reactant that is used up first, determining the maximum amount of product that can form.
Using plants to absorb metal ions from soil; plants are harvested and burned to produce metal-rich ash.
Using bacteria to produce acidic solutions that dissolve metal compounds from low-grade ores.

flashcard_questions.q: After bioleaching, how is the metal recovered from the leachate?
flashcard_questions.a: By displacement using a more reactive metal, or by electrolysis.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one advantage of phytomining over traditional smelting.
flashcard_questions.a: It can extract metals from low-grade ores that are uneconomical to smelt, with lower environmental impact.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the four stages assessed in a life cycle assessment?
flashcard_questions.a: Raw material extraction, manufacturing, use (including transport), and disposal.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might two LCAs of the same product reach different conclusions?
flashcard_questions.a: LCAs involve subjective weighting of factors, and data may be incomplete or selectively presented.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is recycling aluminium particularly worthwhile?
flashcard_questions.a: Extracting aluminium from ore by electrolysis is very energy-intensive; recycling uses a fraction of that energy.

flashcard_questions.q: If a reaction has only one product and no by-products, what is its atom economy?
flashcard_questions.a: 100%, because all reactant atoms end up in the single desired product.

glossary_terms.definition: The percentage of the total mass of all products that is the desired useful product, calculated from the balanced equation.
The actual yield of a product expressed as a percentage of the theoretical maximum yield predicted by the balanced equation.
The reactant that is completely consumed first in a reaction, limiting how much product can form. The other reactant remains in excess.
A systematic analysis of the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its existence, from raw material extraction through to disposal.
A technique that uses certain plants to absorb dissolved metal compounds from soil through their roots. The plants are then harvested and the metal extracted from the ash.
A technique that uses bacteria to produce acidic solutions that dissolve metal compounds from low-grade ores. The dissolved metal can then be extracted by displacement or electrolysis.
